sentences.text: The rule was explained to Tam in the first week, at the bus stop, by a girl called Effie who had appointed herself to the job of explaining things and who was not always accurate.
The rule was that there was a fox in Fernaig wood, and that you only saw it when you were lost.
"Lost how?" "Lost lost.
Off the path, don't know where the road is, that kind." Effie was eating something out of a bag and did not appear to consider any of this remarkable.
"My cousin saw it when he went in after a ball and came out the wrong side by the quarry.
My mum saw it once.

Everybody's seen it once." "Have you?" "No," said Effie, with some annoyance, "because I've lived here my whole life and I can't get lost in it, can I." Tam had moved to Fernaig in the August from a town with a one-way system, and he had not been in the wood, and he filed the fox with the other information he had been given that week: that the shop shut at four on Wednesdays, that you did not sit in the third row on the bus, and that Mr Ross would let you off homework if you asked about the war.
Fernaig had a shop, a school with eighty-one pupils in it, a hall, and a wood that went up the back of everything and did not stop until the forestry track seventeen kilometres north.
It had one bus in the morning and one at half three and a third on Fridays that people spoke about with some ceremony.
It had, as far as Tam could establish in his first fortnight, no way at all of arriving in it.
Everybody there had always been there.
He asked Effie who else had moved in recently and she thought about it seriously for some time and said the Polish family at the sawmill, in 2011.
He saw the fox for the first time on the twelfth of September, in the car park behind the school, at half past three in the afternoon.
It was sitting by the bins, in daylight, in the middle of a village, about five metres from the door he had just come out of.
It was not doing anything.
It was sitting the way a dog sits when it has been told to wait, front legs straight, looking at him.
Tam looked around the car park.

There were two teachers by the minibus and a group from the year above on the wall and Effie's brother locking up a bike, and not one of them had noticed a fox sitting by the bins in the middle of the afternoon.
He looked back and it was still there.
He walked to the bus with his heart going and did not tell anybody, because he had been in that school for four weeks and knew exactly how that conversation would go.
He looked it up that night, which is what you do.

He found that foxes in villages are entirely normal and increasingly common and often bold in daylight, and that this is well documented, and that there was nothing whatsoever remarkable about a fox sitting by some bins.
He read four pages of that and felt better and went to sleep, and in the morning it was on the wall outside the shop.
